prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map shows a top-down egocentric view where the camera wearer's bright chest and extended arms at the bottom (0.1–0.5 m away) reach down toward a wooden table surface roughly 0.6–0.8 m below the camera, with an adjacent lower bench or desk to the left at about 0.9–1.1 m. Four white and light-blue tied plastic bags rest on the table within 0.4–0.8 m of the camera wearer and 0.1–0.3 m of each other, all within arm's reach of the wearer and two other people positioned across the table to the front-top (0.7–1.0 m away, facing toward the table and camera wearer) and to the right (0.5–0.8 m away, facing left toward the table). Across the five frames, the camera tilts slightly upward and rotates clockwise in frames 4 and 5, bringing the upper person's torso (in the 'Jeep' shirt) and the right-side person's green-shirted torso further into view while their heads remain cropped out of frame above and to the right. The depth map clearly separates the vertical layering of the wearer's raised hands, the protruding tied bags, the flat tabletop beneath them, and the darker background floor (>1.5 m away) far better than RGB alone. However, it is unreliable where the right-hand person's arms and torso in frames 4–5 become overly saturated as bright white—appearing closer than the wearer's own hands—and where thin bag ties lose sharp boundary definition.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map labels parts of the scene centered around the wooden table (0.6–0.8 m from the camera wearer), identifying the camera wearer's lower torso and arms at the bottom (0.1–0.5 m away) and partially grouping the two nearby individuals to the front-top (0.7–1.0 m) and right (0.5–0.8 m) who stand about 0.4–0.6 m apart around the table. While the RGB strip shows all three people reaching within arm's reach (0.3–0.5 m) to manipulate the four plastic bags on the table, with the other two people facing inward toward the table and their heads occluded by the top and right frame edges, the segmentation map only detects the 'dining table' in frame 5 and fails to segment any of the bags or the left-hand wooden bench as distinct objects. Across the five frames, as the camera view shifts upward and rightward in frames 4 and 5, the masks for the foreground wearer and surrounding people fragment and shift color assignments. This map highlights coarse foreground-person regions against the unlabelled background, which can help isolate human occupancy on the right and top edges of the frame. However, it is highly unreliable: it merges the plastic bags and parts of the tabletop into the 'person' masks in frames 1–4, mislabels the right person's wristwatch and hand at the right edge of frame 1 as a 'cell phone', splits the camera wearer's own body into multiple conflicting 'person' instances, and places stray 'person' text labels over empty black background on the left.
descriptions.pose: The pose map renders sparse 2D skeletal keypoints on a black background for the people gathered within 0.5–1.0 m of the shared table, where the camera wearer at the bottom faces forward/downward, a second person stands opposite at the top facing the wearer, and a third person sits or stands on the right facing left. In frames 1 and 3, only magenta hand skeletons for the camera wearer's two hands (0.3–0.4 m in front of the camera, within arm's reach of the bags) are detected; in frame 2, both the wearer's lower left hand and the top person's two hands (0.6–0.7 m away at the top) are detected alongside a distorted yellow torso skeleton connecting them; and in frames 4 and 5, the magenta hand skeletons shift to track the top person's two hands (and the wearer's left hand in frame 5) as the camera pans upward. The map makes the fine finger articulations and pinching postures of the detected hands stand out clearly against clutter, even when white hands or bag folds blend together in the RGB image. However, the pose estimation is very unreliable overall: it completely misses the third person on the right in every frame, misses the camera wearer's hands in frame 4 and right hand in frames 2 and 5, and in frame 2 hallucinates a single yellow body skeleton with facial keypoints on the top person's hands and hip keypoints on the camera wearer's wrists because everyone's heads and upper bodies are cropped out of view.
